Evidence is most useful when it is collected as part of the work, not reconstructed weeks later.

Choose one recurring security activity—perhaps reviewing accounts or confirming a maintenance task—and define three things: who performs it, what record shows completion, and who reviews the result. Add a due date and a place for evidence links. Then make the routine small enough to repeat.

We at Cloud2e built the CMMC Tracker to support this operating rhythm. Its recurring maintenance checklist records timestamped completion history, per-item results, evidence links, and reviewer sign-off. The intended benefit is a more consistent trail of the work your team is already responsible for performing.

The tool does not replace technical controls or make changes to the tenant. It organizes records so the program has a clearer system of record.

Pick one recurring activity and ask: could someone else find the latest evidence without searching an inbox?

Evidence maintenance should have a cadence, an owner, and a review step.

A recurring security task is easier to verify when the record captures when it was completed, the result, the supporting evidence, and the reviewer. Without that structure, teams may repeat the work but struggle to locate the latest record when it is needed.

The CLOUD2E CMMC Tracker includes a reusable cybersecurity maintenance checklist with daily-through-annual and event-driven schedules, timestamped run history, evidence links, and reviewer sign-off. It brings that operating record together with assessment, registry, and export capabilities in a system of record deployed within the customer’s GCC High environment.

Start with one recurring activity. Assign the operator and reviewer, define acceptable evidence, and decide how an exception becomes follow-up work. A practical routine should make completion visible without relying on someone’s memory or inbox.
